sources.title: Carbon footprint for the UK and England to 2023

guard_patterns.handling: Require a cited Defra or ONS official source.
Keep territorial, production/residence and consumption bases distinct.
Keep import/export, household-direct and LULUCF boundaries explicit.
Keep MRIO, University of Leeds, Defra and ONS provenance explicit.
Keep MtCO2e, MtCO2, tCO2e/person, shares and years explicit.
Keep 2023 footprint data and July 2026 publication/method versions distinct.
Preserve annual revision status and the 7 July 2026 EU-text correction.
Do not convert national or England aggregates into site, product or parcel measurements.
Never infer parcel emissions from national consumption-account statistics.
Require explicit PASS review for every generated control.

packages.title: 2026 UK GHG three measurement bases QA
facts: UK greenhouse gas emissions are reported on territorial, residence/production and footprint/consumption bases.
Territorial emissions cover emissions that occur within the UK's geographic borders.
Residence or production emissions align with UK National Accounts and attribute emissions to UK residents and businesses.
Footprint or consumption emissions cover emissions associated with UK consumption of goods and services wherever supply-chain emissions occur.
The three measures answer different analytical questions and are intended to be viewed as complementary.
ONS reports 2025 territorial emissions at an estimated 367 MtCO2e.
ONS reports 2024 residence/production emissions provisionally at 478 MtCO2e.
ONS reports 2023 footprint/consumption emissions at 699 MtCO2e.
For 2023, ONS compares territorial emissions at 384 MtCO2e and residence emissions at 480 MtCO2e with the 699 MtCO2e footprint.
Historical estimates for all three measures can be revised when underlying data or methods change.

packages.title: 2026 UK consumption scope export and LULUCF boundary QA
facts: Consumption-based emissions include emissions associated with goods and services consumed by UK residents.
They include emissions occurring overseas in supply chains for imports consumed in the UK.
They include direct household emissions from fossil fuels used for home heating.
They include direct household emissions from fossil fuels used in private vehicles.
Emissions embodied in UK-produced goods that are exported are excluded because those goods are consumed outside the UK.
Land use, land-use change and forestry emissions in the UK are excluded from the carbon-footprint statistics.
Land use, land-use change and forestry emissions abroad are also excluded from the carbon-footprint statistics.
Consumption-based emissions are broader than territorial emissions because they include overseas supply-chain emissions.
The footprint measure is not interchangeable with territorial emissions used for domestic and international target tracking.
The published footprint should not be interpreted as a parcel, site or household-level measurement.

packages.title: 2026 UK carbon-footprint MRIO data-source QA
facts: Defra's UK consumption-based GHG estimates are produced using a multi-regional input-output model.
The model is developed for Defra by the University of Leeds.
The MRIO model combines information on economic activity.
The MRIO model combines trade information.
The MRIO model represents supply-chain relationships.
The MRIO model incorporates greenhouse-gas emissions information.
The model estimates emissions associated with goods and services consumed by UK residents.
The model links flows of goods and services expressed in monetary terms with emissions generated during production.
The model reconciles data from different countries, years, classifications and valuations.
England-level estimates are derived through additional analysis using the same MRIO framework rather than a separate unrelated model.

packages.title: 2026 overseas embedded-emissions uncertainty QA
facts: Emissions embedded in overseas production of UK imports are more difficult to estimate than emissions generated within UK borders.
The release states that internationally recognised methods are used for estimating imported emissions.
Imported-emissions estimates carry greater uncertainty than territorial-emissions estimates.
Defra previously published research on uncertainty in consumption-based CO2 estimates.
That research found relative standard error for total consumption-based CO2 emissions in a year in the range 3.3% to 5.5% for the studied period.
Sector-level errors were generally higher than total-footprint errors in that research.
The methodology has since become more developed.
More up-to-date and reliable financial data are now used than in the earlier uncertainty study.
Methodological improvement does not eliminate the need to preserve uncertainty context when using import-related estimates.
Imported-emissions statistics must not be treated as direct measured emissions from individual imported products or parcels.

packages.title: 2026 UK 2023 carbon-footprint total and trend QA
facts: The UK carbon footprint was estimated at 699 MtCO2e in 2023.
The footprint fell by 4% between 2022 and 2023.
The UK carbon footprint peaked at 984 MtCO2e in 2007.
The 2023 footprint was about 29% below the 2007 peak.
The release reports 826 MtCO2e for 1996.
Embedded emissions from imports totalled 371 MtCO2e in 2023.
2023 imported emissions were 21% below their 2007 peak.
Emissions from UK-produced goods and services consumed domestically were 206 MtCO2e in 2023.
Those domestically produced-and-consumed emissions were 49% lower in 2023 than in 1996.
Percentage changes in the release are calculated from unrounded figures, so calculations from rounded displayed values may differ.

packages.title: 2026 UK consumption emissions per-capita QA
facts: UK consumption-based GHG emissions per capita were estimated at 10 tCO2e per person in 2023.
Per-capita consumption emissions fell by 5% between 2022 and 2023.
Per-capita emissions were 28% lower in 2023 than in 1996.
The per-capita measure peaked at 16 tCO2e per person in 2004.
2023 per-capita emissions were around 37% below the 2004 peak.
Per-capita change differs from total-footprint change because population changes affect the denominator.
Per-capita emissions remained below pre-pandemic levels in 2023.
The 2021 and 2022 data showed a post-COVID-19 bounce back before the latest-year decline.
Per-capita values are national averages rather than measurements for individual people.
The per-capita series remains subject to revisions to underlying footprint estimates and population data.

packages.title: 2026 UK import-share shift QA
facts: Import-related emissions accounted for 31% of the UK carbon footprint in 1996.
Import-related emissions accounted for 53% of the UK carbon footprint in 2023.
Imported emissions therefore represented more than half of the UK's total carbon footprint in 2023.
Emissions associated with UK-produced goods and services consumed domestically represented 29% of total consumption-based emissions in 2023.
Direct household emissions made up the remaining major component of the footprint.
Imported emissions increased substantially over the long term even while total consumption emissions declined.
The shift reflects a growing share of goods and services consumed in the UK being produced overseas.
The UK economy has moved from a stronger manufacturing base toward a service-sector structure since the late 1990s.
Territorial emissions can fall faster than footprint emissions when production moves overseas while UK consumption continues.
The import-share statistic is an aggregate national accounting result and must not be converted into a site or parcel emission factor.

packages.title: 2026 China embedded-import emissions QA
facts: Emissions embedded in UK imports from China were 93 MtCO2e in 2023.
These emissions were more than four times as high in 2023 as in 1996.
China accounted for 25% of UK import-related emissions in 2023.
China accounted for 8% of UK import-related emissions in 1996.
China-related embedded emissions represented 13% of the UK's total carbon footprint in 2023.
They represented about 2% of the total UK carbon footprint in 1996.
Among the source regions discussed in the release, China had the largest absolute embedded-emissions tonnage in 2023.
China also had the largest percentage increase in embedded import emissions since 1996 among the regions highlighted.
China was the only highlighted source region whose embedded import emissions rose during the COVID-19 pandemic.
These estimates describe modeled supply-chain emissions by source region and are not direct product-level measurements.

packages.title: 2026 UK domestic production consumed emissions QA
facts: Emissions from UK-produced goods and services consumed within the UK were 206 MtCO2e in 2023.
They fell slightly from 208 MtCO2e in 2022.
The latest-year fall was about 1%.
These emissions were 49% lower in 2023 than in 1996.
They accounted for 29% of total UK consumption-based emissions in 2023.
This component is different from direct household fossil-fuel emissions.
This component is also different from emissions embedded in imported goods and services.
The category is defined by production in the UK combined with final consumption in the UK.
UK-produced goods that are exported are excluded from the UK consumption footprint.
The national component must not be interpreted as emissions from any individual UK facility without separate site evidence.

packages.title: 2026 direct household heating and private-transport emissions QA
facts: Direct household emissions come from households' use of fossil fuels for heating and personal vehicles.
Direct household emissions were 122 MtCO2e in 2023.
Direct household emissions were 25% lower in 2023 than in 1996.
Direct household emissions accounted for roughly 16% to 20% of total UK consumption-based emissions between 1996 and 2023.
Household heating emissions fluctuate with winter temperatures.
Heating-related emissions were 61 MtCO2e in 2023.
Heating-related emissions were 65 MtCO2e in 2022.
Heating-related emissions have ranged from 61 to 97 MtCO2e since 1996.
Household transport is treated as a separate final-demand category in the published breakdown.
National household totals and averages must not be used as measured household- or parcel-level emission values.

packages.title: 2026 England 2023 carbon-footprint QA
facts: England's carbon footprint was estimated at 587 MtCO2e in 2023.
England's footprint fell by 3% between 2022 and 2023.
England's carbon footprint peaked at 826 MtCO2e in 2007.
The 2023 England footprint was around 29% below that peak.
Emissions from UK-produced goods and services consumed within England were 174 MtCO2e in 2023.
Those domestically produced-and-consumed emissions were 45% lower in 2023 than in 2001.
Direct household emissions in England were 101 MtCO2e in 2023.
England direct household emissions were 25% lower in 2023 than in 2001.
England-level estimates use England-specific household expenditure data and direct household emissions rather than a fixed share of the UK total.
England results remain aggregate consumption-account estimates and not local-authority, site or parcel measurements.

packages.title: 2026 UK and England CO2 footprint QA
facts: CO2 accounted for 78% of the UK's total consumption-based GHG emissions in 2023.
CO2 accounted for 79% of England's total consumption-based GHG emissions in 2023.
The UK's consumption-based CO2 emissions were 548 Mt in 2023.
The UK CO2 footprint was 27% below its 2007 peak of 747 Mt.
The UK CO2 footprint fell by 4% between 2022 and 2023.
England's consumption-based CO2 emissions were 461 Mt in 2023.
England's CO2 footprint was 27% below its 2007 peak of 628 Mt.
England's CO2 footprint fell by 3% between 2022 and 2023.
Defra plans to remove the separate UK and England CO2-footprint measures from the 2027 update, subject to the published feedback process.
The planned 2027 presentation change must not be confused with a change to the 2023 historical values reported in the 2026 release.

packages.title: 2026 territorial production consumption trend-gap QA
facts: Since 1996 the UK carbon footprint decreased by 15%.
Over the same period territorial emissions decreased by 50%.
Over the same period production-based emissions decreased by 42%.
The three measures therefore show materially different long-term rates of decline.
The release links part of this divergence to a shift from manufacturing toward a service-based economy.
Increased reliance on imported goods and services also contributes to the difference.
Consumption-based emissions include imported supply-chain emissions that are outside the UK territorial boundary.
Production-based emissions follow UK residents and businesses rather than only the geographic border.
Territorial, production and consumption measures should not be substituted for each other in target or footprint analysis.
All three time series can be revised as methods and underlying data improve.

packages.title: 2026 FIGARO and EXIOBASE trade-data method switch QA
facts: The 2026 carbon-footprint update made one stated methodological change to the trade-data series.
The update switched to FIGARO v2025 for traded data from 2010 onwards.
Estimates up to 2009 use EXIOBASE v3.8.3 for trade data.
Estimates from 2010 onwards use FIGARO v2025.
The 2025 update also used FIGARO but only for post-2014 estimates.
The 2026 change therefore moves the FIGARO boundary earlier in the time series.
The methodological change can revise historical consumption-emissions estimates.
The publication states that previous-year estimates are subject to revision because of data revisions or methodological improvements.
The UK and England carbon-footprint methodology is expected to continue improving over time.
Method-version boundaries must be preserved when comparing estimates across releases.

packages.title: 2026 carbon-footprint revision and EU correction QA
facts: The release was updated on 7 July 2026 with a correction to the text under Figure 4.
The corrected statement says EU imports accounted for 20% of import-related emissions in 2023.
The corrected statement also says EU imports accounted for 10% of the UK's total carbon footprint in 2023.
The previous wording incorrectly described the 20% figure as a share of the UK's total carbon footprint.
EU-related embedded emissions were 72 MtCO2e in 2023.
The EU was the second-largest source of import-related GHG emissions in 2023 among the regions discussed.
EU import-related emissions were 22% lower in 2023 than in 2019.
The release states that estimates for previous years are subject to revision.
Percentage changes are calculated from unrounded values, so displayed rounded figures may not exactly reproduce them.
Any downstream QA or web display must preserve the corrected 20%-of-imports and 10%-of-total distinction.
